## The rules of the studio
- The easel is the only way to paint and to see the painting. Don't replay
  or copy the session yourself, open a second one, or edit or restore its
  files. (`bin/easel check`, which verifies the log against the canvas, is
  fine.)
- Look at the canvas with the easel's views. Don't read pixel values with
  other programs.
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A reflection in water is painted as its own shape, not as
  `mask:at(x, 2*h - y)`.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `bin/easel note "..."` as you go: your own
  working notes. Add to it; don't rewrite earlier entries.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete. Then save it
  (`bin/easel save`) and close the session.

## When you're done
Reply with the paths of the saved painting and its log, the painting's
title if you give it one, and if you like a few sentences about the
picture.

`io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `bin/easel note '<text>'` (or
`bin/easel note -` to read the text from stdin) appends an entry stamped
with the session's painting time, such as `day 2, 09:40`; the session must
be open. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

## The log

`bin/easel check` replays the log in a fresh session and compares it with
the live canvas. The log, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, is plain Lua with
a line `--@ chunk N` before each chunk. The easel keeps a record of it in
`out/easel/painting/committed.lua`. If the log is changed, shortened or
missing, the easel refuses to continue.

    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

unds, which gives about 5–16 mm. A mock-up cycled between 95% and 20% RH showed about 9 corner cracks with **6 ± 3 mm** spacing [21][V].
- Oil paint layer on panel, model: **S/t ≈ 4** (egg tempera about 3) [22][V]. For a 50–120 µm paint film that means 0.2–0.5 mm micro-cracking [E].

**Pattern features (Bucklow).** Bucklow used seven features: predominant direction; local jaggedness vs. global curvature; junction and termination type; the relationship between directions; distance between cracks; crack thickness; and network organization [18][V][20]. Patterns differ enough between groups of paintings that human sorters and a discriminant analysis on Bézier-coded cracks could tell the groups apart [19][V].
- **Weave coupling depends on the ground.** "Jagged cracks with a rectangular pattern are associated with characteristically thin brittle grounds which allow cracks to faithfully follow the (plain) canvas weave. Smooth, curved cracks are associated with thick (possibly double) grounds", which "liberate" the pattern from the canvas [18][V].

**About the picture.** A dark-ground still life in the old manner: a shallow ochre bowl holding three apples — red, yellow-green, red — with two more on a pale cloth in front of it, on a dark table against a wall that keeps a warm glow in its upper left corner. Studio notes from this campaign, for next time:

- `work` with a *hard-edged* rect/glow mask leaves a visible rectangle. Always feather well outside the damaged area.
- An option table with only string keys has no array part, so table.unpack(t) returns NOTHING and every option is silently dropped. Write options out, or keep the array part.

- blend(m) leaves a hard disc if the mask is a shrunk copy of the shape — use (m:shrink(3)):soften(3).
- blend() over a lean layer lifts the lead-white ground through in pale blobs. It needs a thick opaque base under it first, and even then only twice.
- Never blend a whole group of touching objects: it drags one fruit's colour onto the next.
- Surgical fix-ups with masks that cross other objects do more harm than the flaw. Repaint the object instead.
EOF

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

**Value plan** (what a Chardin/Heda-like still life needs):

2. The modelling shapes: use *elliptical zones that are concentric-ish with the fruit* so the gradient is spherical. The cleanest: for a sphere, the value at a point depends on the dot product with the light. A painter approximates with 3-4 zones whose boundaries are arcs concentric with the sphere's silhouette. Repainted the whole picture from the dark ground up and this time I judge it finished: a shallow earthenware bowl with three apples (two red, one green), a red and a green apple in front on a white cloth, a dark warm wall, one soft light from the upper left. Title: "Apples in an Earthenware Bowl".

What the repainting taught me, all of it the hard way:
- COVERAGE IS NOT OPACITY. A pass at coverage 2-3 is a veil. To bury a strong old colour (saturated vermilion) I had to go to coverage 8-10 in two passes. The same pile over a pale cloth comes out much lighter and more saturated than the same pile over a dark ground, because the film is thin - so a pile has to be mixed against the ground it will sit on, not judged on the palette.
- The recipe that works for a solid coat: hand="broad" (or a big filbert), coverage 3-4.5, fill=true, pressure 1, dips={1,1.0,0.0} so every stroke gets a full load. With dips={3,...} the load runs out along the stroke and I get starved streaks. Then ONE blend over the opaque coat to fuse the strokes, and no more blending after that.
- THIN FILMS BLOOM. Any small, thin or low-coverage application of a lead-white or vermilion pile over a dark ground glows like a lamp - I made three separate glowing highlights and had to paint them out. For a highlight on a dark form either lay the fruit'"'"'s own light colour more thickly, or use a lead-white-free earth. fill=true over a small mask beads the paint into cottage cheese; a single touch is the only clean way to lay a small light spot.
- A sphere reads from lay-in, terminator, core shadow and a quiet reflected light. It does not need a specular highlight, and it certainly does not need a hard edge-light along the silhouette - that read as a drawn outline and had to be painted out.
- Colour: raw umber is a LIGHT earth, so "umber + black" is still mid-value, and yellow ochre + red earth is a pumpkin, not earthenware. Earthenware wants raw umber + red earth + a little lead white and nothing bright.
- Paint order matters absolutely. I laid cloth passes that painted straight over the fruit and the bowl and had to repaint the group. All cloth work now goes through free = cloth - bowl - fruit, and the fruit are painted last.
- `below(600)` is an error - below() wants a curve or a point list, not a number. That one cost me three failed chunks.
- A contact shadow must be a pool just under the object and offset away from the light, not a ring around its base; a ring reads as dirt. Same for a ring-shaped highlight.
- Long thin accent strokes (a filbert 6 with an explicit stroke and clip) are the one thing that stays crisp - I finished with fold lines on the cloth and a thin light on the bowl'"'"'s rim laid that way.
- A glaze of a warm dark over the group and a cool dark over the room tied the whole picture together and gave the darks their depth.'

LX, LY = -0.50, -0.866   -- toward the light: up and to the left
function cosf(cx, cy, rx, ry, x, y)
  local u = (x - cx) / rx; local v = (y - cy) / ry

function litm(cx, cy, rx, ry, t0, t1)
  return mask(function(x, y) return smoothstep(t0, t1, cosf(cx, cy, rx, ry, x, y)) end)
end

function litf(a, t0, t1)
  return mask(function(x, y)

    return smoothstep(t0, t1, (u * LX + v * LY) / r)
  end)

function corem(a, t0, t1) return litf(a, t0, t1):map(function(v) return 1 - v end) end
function fruit(a, lay, mid, lit, hi, core, sd, k, ct)
  k = k or 1
  local S = ellipse(a.cx, a.cy, a.r, a.r * 0.95):roughen(2.5, 70, sd):soften(2.5)
  local tool = "filbert " .. math.max(9, math.floor(a.r / 5))
  work(S, {hand="body", tool=tool, pile=lay, length={30, 80}, coverage=4.5*k, pressure=1,
           fill=true, dips={1, 1.0, 0.0}, edge="found"})
  work(S * litf(a, 0.0, 0.55), {hand="body", tool=tool, pile=mid, length={30, 80}, coverage=3.2*k,
           pressure=1, fill=true, dips={1, 1.0, 0.0}, edge="soft"})
  work(S * litf(a, 0.45, 0.95), {hand="body", tool=tool, pile=lit, length={30, 80}, coverage=3.0*k,
           pressure=1, fill=true, dips={1, 1.0, 0.0}, edge="soft"})
  blend(S:rim(20, 14), {angle=0.3})
  work(S * corem(a, -0.9, ct or 0.3), {hand="body", tool=tool, pile=core, length={30, 80},
           coverage=4.0*k, pressure=1, fill=true, dips={1, 1.0, 0.0}, edge="soft"})
  blend(S:rim(15, 10), {angle=0.3})
  work(S:rim(a.r * 0.08, 5) * corem(a, -0.6, 0.2) * ellipse(a.cx, a.cy + a.r * 0.9, a.r * 0.7, a.r * 0.42),
       {hand="glaze", pile=g_cm, coverage=0.6})
  stipple(hoff(a, 0.52):blur(a.r * 0.15), {pile=hi, width=4, coverage=2.6,
         pressure={0.5, 0.8}, cluster=0.3, dips={5, 1.0, 0.3}})
end
